title: Jaw
description: Pathology of the maxilla and mandible — odontogenic and non-odontogenic cysts, jaw tumours, fibro-osseous diseases, deep-space infections, maxillary sinus problems, and dento-alveolar / facial-skeleton fractures.

problems.description: Cheek pain and tenderness over the upper molars, worse on moving the head, with nasal stuffiness on the same side.
problems.etiology: Usually follows a viral upper respiratory tract infection that reduces cilia activity, allowing bacterial superinfection — typically mixed flora including anaerobes, Haemophilus, staphylococci, and streptococci [1]. Less commonly caused by a foreign body such as a displaced root [1]. Poor drainage via the ostium exacerbates the situation [1]. The maxillary antra are the largest of the four paired paranasal sinuses, lying in each half of the maxilla between the alveolus inferiorly, nasal cavity medially, and orbits superiorly [2].
problems.presentation: Pain and tenderness over the cheeks, nasal discharge or stuffiness, and pain worse on moving the head [3]. Antral symptoms often mimic pathology attributable to maxillary teeth, so dental causes must be excluded first [3].
problems.results: Occipito-mental X-rays (15° and 30°) may reveal antral opacity, fluid level, or fracture [3]. To define a fluid level, the film is repeated with the head tilted [3]. CT scans are used for tumours, pansinusitis, and blow-out fractures [3].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Pain worsens on head movement or bending forward. Diagnosis is by exclusion of dental pathology, nasal discharge, cheek tenderness, and head-position-dependent pain [3]. Confirmed by proof puncture if necessary [1].
problems.treatment: Erythromycin 500 mg PO qds or doxycycline 100 mg PO od [1]. Decongestants such as oxymetazoline or xylometazoline spray [1]. For chronic sinusitis with poor drainage: foreign bodies removed via an incision in the canine fossa and creation of a bony window into the antrum (Caldwell–Luc approach); ventilation by intranasal antrostomy or functional endoscopic sinus surgery [4].
problems.prognosis: Acute sinusitis resolves with antibiotics and decongestants in most cases. Chronic sinusitis may develop if a foreign body or poor drainage persists; mucosal lining hypertrophies and may form polyps [4]. A post-nasal drip is often present in chronic cases [4].

Occipito-mental X-rays (15° and 30°) may reveal antral opacity, fluid level, or # (…… Nasal and malar fractures, p. 498). To define fluid level, repeat film with head tilted. Chronic sinusitis may then develop, particularly if a foreign body or poor drainage is present. Mucosal lining hypertrophies and may form polyps. A post-nasal discharge (drip) is often present. Rx: aimed at re-ventilation of the sinus. Foreign bodies, if present, should be removed via an incision in the canine fossa (above the premolars) and creation of a bony window into the antrum (Caldwell–Luc approach).

problems.description: Inability to bring the teeth together after facial trauma, with lingual haematoma, step deformity along the jaw, and possibly numb lower lip.
problems.etiology: The commonest fracture of the facial skeleton [1]. Most result from fights and road traffic accidents [1]. Rarely comminuted with hard and soft tissue loss, as in gunshot wounds [1]. Condylar neck fractures are the commonest subtype; angle fractures usually occur through the wisdom-tooth socket, and body fractures commonly through the canine socket [2].
problems.presentation: Inability to bite the teeth or dentures together in the normal way [3]. A lingual mucosal haematoma is pathognomonic of a mandibular fracture [3]. Bruising and swelling over the fracture site, sometimes lacerations [3]. Displaced fractures may cause gagging on the posterior teeth with the mouth hanging open [3]. Saliva is usually bloodstained [3]. Paraesthesia in the distribution of the IDN may be reported by the patient [3]. Gentle palpation reveals step deformities, bony crepitus, and tenderness [3]. All have trismus to some degree, opening less than 40 mm [3].
problems.results: DPT and PA mandible are the essential radiographs to diagnose and assess a mandibular fracture [4]. CT scans are required to assess condylar fractures before fixation [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Inability to occlude combined with lingual mucosal haematoma is pathognomonic [3]. Step deformities palpable in the lingual and buccal sulcus [5]. Gentle bilateral pressure over the angles of the mandible produces pain even with a crack fracture [5].
problems.treatment: Most patients are admitted to hospital, nursed sitting up and leaning forward [6]. Nil by mouth with IV crystalloid for hydration [6]. Compound fractures require antibiotics [6]. Analgesia via LA, temporary circumdental bridle wire, parenteral NSAIDs, or opioids as needed [6]. Definitive treatment: open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with small bone plates and monocortical screws via mucosal incisions [7]. Condylar fractures in patients over 12 years: establish pain-free pre-injury occlusion by elastic traction, reassess at 7 days; if not achieved, proceed to ORIF [8].
problems.prognosis: Condylar fractures in children under 12 years treated with analgesia, soft diet, and intermaxillary elastic guidance produce optimal results [8]. Teeth in the fracture line can often be preserved with antibiotics, adequate reduction, and endodontics as a secondary procedure [7].

citations.quote: These are the commonest # of the facial skeleton (Fig. 12.1). Most are the result of fights and road traffic accidents (the former ubiquitous in Western countries whereas the latter are commoner in the Middle East; the role of alcohol, laws, and attitudes to driving are self-evident). Rarely, they may be comminuted with hard and soft tissue loss, e.g. gunshot wounds.

Condylar neck # are commonest and range from easiest to most difficult. Often found with a # of the angle or canine region of the opposite side of the jaw. Rarely, bilateral condylar # is found with a symphyseal #—'guardsman's #' from falling on the point of the chin. Angle # usually occurs through wisdom-tooth socket, and body # commonly through canine socket.

History of trauma. Ask if the patient can bite their teeth or dentures together in the manner which is normal to them. Inability to do this and a lingual mucosal haematoma is pathognomonic of a mandibular #. Look at the face; there is usually bruising and swelling over the # site and sometimes lacerations. If the # is displaced, there may be gagging on the posterior teeth and the mouth hangs open. The saliva is usually bloodstained. The patient may complain of paraesthesia in the distribution of the IDN. Gentle palpation over the mandible will reveal step deformities, bony crepitus, and tenderness. All have trismus to some degree, opening <40mm.

DPT and PA mandible are the essentials in order to diagnose and assess a mandibular fracture. Most patients in trauma centres will have additional assessment with a CT scan. CT scans are required to assess condylar fractures before fixation.

This may reveal broken teeth or dentures which should be removed. Suction the mouth to clean away blood clots prior to examining both the buccal and lingual sulcus. Look for step deformities in the occlusion, and examine the teeth. Palpate for steps in the lingual and buccal sulcus. If ∆ is uncertain, it is sometimes worth trying to elicit abnormal mobility across the suspected # site, using gentle pressure. In cases where you are very unsure, place one hand over each angle of the mandible and exert gentle pressure; this will produce pain if there is a #, even if it is only a crack #.

Most patients will be admitted to hospital, nursed sitting up and leaning forward as this is the most comfortable position. Keep nil by mouth and maintain hydration by IV crystalloid. Compound # need antibiotics. Assess need for analgesia; LA, temporary immobilization with circumdental wire (bridle wire), parenteral NSAIDs, or opioids may be needed.

# sites are exposed, usually via mucosal incisions, and reduced under direct vision; the teeth are placed in temporary IMF &/or a wire around the tooth on either side of the # (tension band or bridle wire) and small bone plates fixed by monocortical screws are placed to immobilize the reduction.

>12yrs: pain-free, pre-injury occlusion should be established (by elastic traction if need be), and the patient reassessed at 7 days. If spontaneous pain-free occlusion not possible at this stage: ORIF.

problems.description: Fluid or air passing between the mouth and nose after upper molar extraction, with reflux of liquids into the nasal cavity on drinking.
problems.etiology: A communication between the maxillary antrum and the oral cavity created during root removal [1]. The proximity of maxillary cheek teeth to the antral floor makes it easy for roots and even teeth to be displaced into the antrum and predisposes to fracture of the alveolar process during extraction [2]. When the communication persists and becomes lined by epithelium, it becomes a fistula [3].
problems.presentation: Post-extraction reflux of fluids into the nose or minor nosebleeds are diagnostic pointers [3]. Confirmed by asking the patient to attempt to blow out against a closed nose: air bubbles through the fistula [3]. Occasionally, antral mucosa prolapses through the socket [3].
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis confirmed by the closed-nose blow test [3]. Occipito-mental X-rays or DPT may show antral changes or a retained root [4].
problems.definingCharacteristics: A pathological epithelium-lined tract between the mouth and maxillary sinus [3]. Most often follows extraction of isolated molar teeth [3]. The tendency to persist distinguishes fistula from a simple communication that closes spontaneously [3].
problems.treatment: If diagnosed at time of extraction: close the socket by suture or buccal advancement flap, give antibiotics and decongestants as for maxillary sinusitis, and advise the patient not to blow the nose [3]. If diagnosed more than 2 days after extraction: place on antibiotics and decongestants for 2 weeks and review after 6 weeks [3]. If still open, repair by buccal advancement flap — excise the fistula, reflect a broad-based full-thickness buccal flap, incise periosteum to allow the mucosa to stretch over the socket, and close with vertical mattress sutures over bone [5]. Alternatively, palatal rotation flap based on the palatine artery, or buccal fat pad flap [6, 7]. Decongestants: ephedrine nasal drops 0.5–1%, 1–2 drops into the relevant nostril qds for 7–10 days [8]. Patient referred to oral surgery if the GDP cannot carry out closure [1].
problems.prognosis: Many small fistulae are asymptomatic and close spontaneously [3]. Persistent fistulae require surgical closure; buccal advancement flap is reliable but may reduce sulcus depth [5].

citations.quote: This is a complication that can occur during root removal, whereby a communication between the maxillary antrum and the oral cavity is created. If the root is removed, then the operator should close the communication with local full-depth mucoperiosteal flaps. If not able to carry out this procedure, a referral should be made to the local oral surgery department. The patient should be encouraged to avoid blowing their nose until resolved and a nasal decongestant prescribed (0.5% ephedrine nasal drops for 5 days).

The proximity of maxillary cheek teeth to the antral floor makes it easy for roots and even teeth to be displaced into the antrum. It also predisposes to # of the alveolar process during 6, 7, 8 extraction.

This is the creation of a pathological epithelium-lined tract between the mouth and maxillary sinus. This most often occurs following the extraction of isolated molar teeth when the fistula tends to persist. Post-extraction reflux of fluids into the nose or minor nosebleeds are diagnostic pointers. Confirm by getting the patient to attempt to blow out against a closed nose; air bubbles through the fistula. Occasionally, antral mucosa prolapses through the socket. Rx: many small fistulae are asymptomatic and close spontaneously. Closure if ∆ is made at the time of extraction: close the socket by suture or buccal advancement flap (Fig. 10.13), give antibiotics and decongestants as for maxillary sinusitis, and advise not to blow the nose. Closure if ∆ is made >2 days after extraction: place on antibiotics, etc., for 2 weeks and review after 6 weeks.

Often mimics symptoms attributable to maxillary teeth. ∆ is by exclusion of dental pathology, nasal discharge or stuffiness, tenderness over the cheeks, and pain worse on moving the head. Occipito-mental X-rays (15° and 30°) may reveal antral opacity, fluid level, or #. To define fluid level, repeat film with head tilted. Other X-rays: DPT for cysts and roots and CT scans for tumours, pansinusitis, and blow-out #.

Buccal advancement flap—excise fistula to prepare a line of closure over bone and raise a broad-based buccal flap. Incise periosteum to allow mucosa to stretch over the socket and close, over bone, with vertical mattress sutures. Use antibiotics, etc., remove sutures at 10 days. Disadvantages: thin tissue may break down; reduces sulcus depth.

Palatal rotation flap—excise fistula as for buccal advancement flap. Dissect a palatal mucoperiosteal flap based on palatine artery, rotate over socket, and suture in similar fashion (Fig. 10.14). Disadvantages: bare bone left to granulate; difficult flap to rotate without distortion.

Buccal fat pad flap—if after raising the buccal advancement flap the periosteal incision is opened with artery forceps, the buccal fat pad is exposed. This can be easily mobilized as a pedicled flap to suture into and obtund the defect.

Dose: ephedrine nasal drops 0.5–1%, 1–2 drops into the relevant nostril qds for 7–10 days. For symptomatic nasal decongestion and as an adjunct to the management of oro-antral fistulae inhalation of menthol and eucalyptus is valuable.

problems.description: Painless buccal expansion of the jaw around an unerupted tooth found on routine X-ray, with delayed eruption of the associated permanent tooth.
problems.etiology: Forms around the crown of an unerupted permanent tooth and arises from reduced enamel epithelium [1]. May delay eruption of the associated tooth [1].
problems.presentation: Typically a painless swelling causing buccal expansion of the jaw, or an incidental radiolucent finding on X-ray associated with an unerupted tooth crown. May delay or prevent normal eruption [1].
problems.results: Radiolucent area on X-ray enveloping the crown of an unerupted tooth. Cyst lining should always be submitted for histopathology [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Arises specifically from reduced enamel epithelium around the crown of an unerupted permanent tooth [1]. Distinguished from inflammatory (radicular) cysts by its association with an unerupted tooth rather than a necrotic pulp [3].
problems.treatment: Marsupialization or enucleation, depending on the position and desired fate of the tooth [1]. Marsupialization opens the cyst to create continuity with oral mucosa and is useful when enucleation is contraindicated or when tooth eruption through the cyst is desired [4]. Cyst lining must always be submitted for histopathology [2].
problems.prognosis: Enucleation is curative. Marsupialization is slower to heal and leaves a cavity for some time but allows the associated tooth to erupt [4].

citations.quote: These form around the crown of an unerupted permanent tooth and arise from reduced enamel epithelium. May delay eruption. Rx: marsupialization or enucleation, depending on position and desired fate of the tooth.
Always submit cyst lining for histopathology.

These are very common, and may also be called radicular cysts. Described as apical or lateral depending on position in relation to tooth root, or residual if left behind after tooth extraction. Necrotic pulp is the stimulus, and the epithelium comes from cell rests of Malassez.

Marsupialization. This is the opening of the cyst to allow continuity with the oral mucosa; healing is slower than with enucleation and a cavity persists for some time. It is useful to allow tooth eruption through the cyst or where enucleation is C/I.

problems.description: Slowly expanding swelling of the posterior lower jaw, more common in men and those of African descent, expanding the cortex rather than perforating it.
problems.etiology: One of the commoner odontogenic tumours [1]. Commonest in men and Africans, and in the posterior mandible [1]. There are three basic types: unicystic, polycystic, and peripheral [1]. The unicystic type is the least aggressive; the polycystic and peripheral types show a tendency to invade surrounding tissue, whereas the unicystic expands it [1]. Metastases are very rare [1].
problems.presentation: Slow-growing, painless expansion of the posterior mandible. The unicystic type expands bone; the polycystic and peripheral types invade surrounding tissue [1]. Histologically, two patterns are seen: plexiform and follicular [1].
problems.results: Radiolucent lesion on X-ray; the multiloculated appearance may be confused with a keratocyst [2]. Histology distinguishes the two.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Commonest in the posterior mandible in men and in people of African descent [1]. Three subtypes with differing behaviour: unicystic (least aggressive, expands), polycystic and peripheral (invade) [1]. Metastases very rare [1].
problems.treatment: Unicystic type: enucleation provided a rim of enclosing bone is also removed [1]. Polycystic and peripheral types: excision with a margin [1].
problems.prognosis: Recurrence risk is higher for polycystic and peripheral types due to tissue invasion; excision with a margin is required [1]. Unicystic type has lower recurrence risk after enucleation with rim of bone [1]. Metastases are very rare [1].

citations.quote: One of the commoner odontogenic tumours. Commonest in men and Africans, and in the posterior mandible. There are three basic types: unicystic, polycystic, and peripheral. The unicystic type is the least aggressive; the polycystic and peripheral types show a tendency to invade surrounding tissue, whereas the unicystic expands it. Metastases are very rare. Histologically, two types are seen: plexiform and follicular. Rx: unicystic can be enucleated provided a rim of enclosing bone is removed as well; the other types require excision with a margin.
Their multiloculated appearance on X-ray may confuse them with an ameloblastoma.

problems.description: Exposed, non-healing jaw bone in a patient taking anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic medication, often following a tooth extraction.
problems.etiology: Several anti-resorptive and anti-angiogenic drugs prescribed in the UK have been associated with MRONJ, but it is most commonly due to bisphosphonates [1]. Bisphosphonates act by inhibiting osteoclast function; they bind to hydroxyapatite and their effect is extremely long-term, possibly up to 10 years [2]. They come in differing degrees of potency: non-nitrogen-containing oral preparations are least potent; nitrogen-containing IV preparations are most potent [3]. Denosumab — a human monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclast formation, function, and survival — and anti-angiogenic drugs such as bevacizumab, sunitinib, and aflibercept also carry the potential to cause bone necrosis [4]. The principle underlying the risk is that surgery requiring osteoclast activity for healing cannot proceed safely in patients taking these drugs [1].
problems.presentation: Alveolar bone exposed in the mouth in a patient taking anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic medication [5]. May be painful or painless. Non-healing extraction socket is a common trigger. Bone necrosis without mucosal breach is also described [5].
problems.results: Clinical diagnosis: exposed necrotic bone in the jaw in a patient on relevant medication. The condition appears progressive and there is no established effective treatment [5].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Exposed alveolar bone in the jaw associated with anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic drug use [5]. Usually (although not always) associated with extractions or dento-alveolar surgery [5]. Incidence ranges from much less than 1% for low-potency drugs in osteoporosis to up to 30% for myeloma survivors at 10 years who have received highly potent drugs and had extractions [5].
problems.treatment: Risk is assessed before any surgery; aim to avoid surgery requiring osteoclast activity for healing [1]. If extraction is unavoidable: warn the patient of risks (range from <1% for low-risk drug in osteoporosis to 30% in a myeloma survivor at 10 years), use prophylactic chlorhexidine and broad-spectrum antibiotic, atraumatic extraction, alveolar septoplasty to ensure all bone lies well below the gingival margin, and close mucosa primarily [6]. For established MRONJ: limited sequestrectomy with coverage of exposed bone; refer to local oral and maxillofacial surgery [7].
problems.prognosis: There are no agreed effective treatments for established MRONJ to date [7]. Tactics that work for osteoradionecrosis do not seem to help [7]. Prevention is the most useful management strategy [8].

citations.quote: Several anti-resorptive and anti-angiogenic drugs that are prescribed in the UK have been associated with MRONJ but commonly it is due to bisphosphonates. Risk assessment is required and the Rx needs to be tailored according to the risk. The principle is not to carry out any surgery which requires osteoclast activity for healing on someone taking these drugs.

Bisphosphonates constitute a wide group of agents which act primarily by inhibiting osteoclast function which helps prevent fractures in osteoporosis, stabilizes Paget's disease, relieves bone pain and fractures in bone metastases in a range of malignancies, and can treat hypercalcaemia of carcinomatosis. Unfortunately, one of their side effects is necrosis of jaw bone, usually (although not always) associated with extractions or dento-alveolar surgery.

They come in differing degrees of potency, non-nitrogen-containing oral preparations being the least potent and nitrogen-containing IV preparations being the most potent. Osteoporosis tends to be managed with less potent drugs and hypercalcaemia and bone metastases with the most.

Denosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that inhibits osteoclast formation, function, and survival. It is used in the treatment of osteoporosis, bone metastasis, and a number of other conditions that result in ↑ bone turnover. It is only available in IV form and is considered a million times more potent than etidronate. Denosumab and other non-bisphosphonate drugs such as anti-angiogenic drugs bevacizumab, sunitinib, and aflibercept still have the potential to cause bone necrosis. This is known as 'medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw' or 'MRONJ'.

Bisphosphonate-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (BRONJ aka BRON aka anti-resorptive-related osteonecrosis of the jaws (ARONJ)) is a condition where alveolar bone is exposed in the mouth in patients taking these drugs. The condition appears to be progressive and there is no established effective treatment although several are being investigated. Bone necrosis without mucosal breach is also described. The incidence is variable but is probably much less than 1% for patients treated with low-potency drugs for osteoporosis, up to 30% for myeloma survivors at 10yrs who have received highly potent drugs and who have had extractions.

If this can be avoided by endodontics, coronectomy, etc. then do it. If not, warn the patient of risks (range from <1% for low-risk drug in osteoporosis patient to 30% in a myeloma survivor at 10yrs). Use prophylactic chlorhexidine and broad-spectrum antibiotic, atraumatic extraction, and alveolar septoplasty to ensure all bone lies well below the gingival margin and close mucosa primarily.

There are no agreed effective Rxs to date. Tactics that work for osteoradionecrosis do not seem to help. Limited sequestrectomy coupled with some form of coverage of the exposed bone seems to help and a variety of supplemental drug Rxs are being used but there is no established evidence base for this. Refer to your local oral and maxillofacial surgery department.

Prevention is the most useful management strategy and all patients prior to starting bisphosphonates should have optimum dental health established such that it is highly unlikely they will ever need to have a tooth removed in the future.
